DSO 510 · Final analysis · Paris Airbnb

Pricing the Games

Are higher nightly prices associated with lower occupancy, and did that relationship differ between July–August 2023 and July–August 2024? These observational estimates do not establish causation or identify an optimal price for Los Angeles.

Pooled price cutoff

Cutoff calculated once across the full valid July–August 2023/2024 sample, then applied unchanged to both periods.

Full valid sample: native nightly price; dashed marker is pooled q99

99th-percentile cutoff: €1,090.58 per night. This removes 212 of 21,172 valid rows (1.00% — just over 1% because of quantile ties), leaving 20,960 rows and 8,127 listings for primary analysis.

Presentation wording

In the primary sample, excluding listing-month prices above the pooled q99 cutoff, mean recorded gross revenue per listing-month was €2,482.08 in 2023 and €2,216.50 in 2024, a change of -€265.58 (-10.7%); mean gross revenue per calendar night was €80.07 versus €71.50 (8,489 listing-months in 2023; 12,471 in 2024). These are observational comparisons of recorded gross revenue, not profit or evidence that price changes caused revenue to change. For LA 2028 hosts, the comparison highlights that higher nightly prices alone do not guarantee higher gross receipts; costs, availability, booking timing, and local demand matter, and Paris does not identify an optimal LA price. Among 2,352 listings observed in all four months, mean recorded gross revenue per listing-month was €3,189.12 in 2023 and €2,654.48 in 2024, a change of -€534.64 (-16.8%); mean gross revenue per calendar night was €102.87 versus €85.63 after averaging July and August within each listing-year. These are observational comparisons of recorded gross revenue, not profit or evidence that price changes caused revenue to change. For LA 2028 hosts, the comparison highlights that higher nightly prices alone do not guarantee higher gross receipts; costs, availability, booking timing, and local demand matter, and Paris does not identify an optimal LA price.

For LA 2028 hosts, this adds a gross-revenue comparison alongside occupancy, but it cannot show that price changes caused the revenue pattern. Paris does not identify an optimal LA price.

Interpretation, hypotheses, and limitations

Observed findings

Models 1 and 2 show small, statistically uncertain price slopes. In Model 3, the trimmed-sample price slopes are positive in both periods: +1.753 pp per €100 in 2023 and +0.828 in 2024. The 2024-minus-2023 difference is −0.925 pp (p=.039; CI −1.802 to −0.048). That is opposite a simple negative price–occupancy hypothesis, but it is not causal evidence. The matched four-month primary interaction is +0.460 pp (p=0.441; CI -0.711 to +1.631), not statistically clear.

Theory-based expectations

Event demand and fewer substitutes might weaken price sensitivity, while added supply or overpricing could strengthen a negative association. These competing expectations were theory-based, not preregistered; the full-sample comparison also demonstrates sensitivity to extreme prices.

Currency and control assumptions

Selected records state EUR. We use native_avg_daily_rate as euros/night, retaining avg_daily_rate for comparison because fields differ and file-specific documentation is incomplete. Entire-home is the control because property type can relate to both price and demand. Bedrooms has about 13% missing and extreme values, so it is not used.

Limitations

Monthly records do not isolate event dates. Year samples differ in composition. Location and property quality may raise both prices and bookings, biasing the observed price association upward (less negative). Availability, timing, amenities, and host strategy are unobserved; listing-clustered errors do not remove confounding. These results do not estimate a causal effect or an optimal LA price.
